items.title: Aureka seals $8.9M deal to vault into Victorian gold production
paras: Advertisement Sponsored Business Companies Bulls N' Bears Aureka seals $8.9M deal to vault into Victorian gold production Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS

Share A A A Aureka Limited has officially completed a transformational $8.9 million acquisition that instantly elevates the company from a Victorian gold explorer to a fully fledged producer. The deal delivers ownership of the producing Fiddlers Creek underground gold-silver mine and the strategically valuable Wedderburn processing mill.

Notably, the assets have generated positive monthly free cash flow since the June quarter, according to the unaudited accounts. Completed on November 13, the deal to purchase High Grade Holdings, owner of Fiddlers Creek and Wedderburn, comprised $2.5M cash and $6.4M in shares, backed by a $7.65M two-tranche capital raise.

High Grade Holdings founder Toby Houldsworth (right) hands over the keys to Aureka Limited’s new mining superintendent Jason Oosthuizen at the Fiddlers Creek underground gold-silver mine in Victoria. Up to $2M more is payable through four $500,000 milestones. Three require cumulative gold output through Wedderburn of 900 ounces within 12 months, 2500 within 24 months and 4000 within 36 months. The fourth covers Fiddlers Creek resource and reserve estimates, mining licence approval and expanded mill tailings capacity.

Wedderburn could rapidly become the jewel in Aureka’s crown. One of just six gold processing mills in Victoria licensed to treat third-party ore, the fully permitted plant is currently ticking over at just 20 per cent of its 42,000-tonne annual capacity, based on 80 per cent uptime, leaving plenty of room to ramp things up, including a potentially lucrative toll-treatment business.

However, the bigger prize could lie in Aureka’s own backyard. The company is eyeing a hub-and-spoke operation that would funnel ore from its growing stable of Victorian gold projects through Wedderburn, potentially turning the underutilised mill into the beating heart of a much bigger regional gold business.

The first spoke is operating. Fiddlers Creek, in Victoria’s historic Percydale goldfield near Avoca, restarted underground production in July 2025. In the year to June 2026, it recovered 416 ounces from ore averaging seven grams per tonne (g/t) gold, with recoveries averaging 86 per cent and peaking at 91 per cent.

The geological upside is tantalising. Legacy drilling delivereddownhole hits of 0.06m at an eye-watering 786.1g/t gold and 0.35m at 1.6kg/t silver. Surrounding tenure spans 39 square kilometres, six mineralised trends and more than 600 historic workings.

Aureka Limited managing director James Gurry said: “Completing the acquisition of High Grade Holdings is a defining moment for Aureka. We now own and operate the Fiddlers Creek mine and the Wedderburn Mill, which moves us from explorer to producer, with current production and a processing pathway for our broader Victorian portfolio.”
With extra staff and working capital, management is ramping up both operations.

At Fiddlers Creek, the drill bit is turning on a 400-metre diamond drilling campaign, the first from surface since May 2025, chasing extensions to known high-grade gold zones and looking to add fresh ounces beyond the existing mine plan.

The work forms part of a minimum 1800m drilling commitment over three years. Fiddlers Creek operates under a prospecting licence, approved work plan and planning permit, with a mining licence application pending. Meanwhile, Aureka is eyeing further opportunities at Wedderburn, including making better use of its existing mining licence footprint, expanding tailings capacity and securing additional ore to feed the underutilised mill.

Next cab off the rank could be Aureka’s Comstock gold-silver project near St Arnaud, 45km southwest of Wedderburn. The former mine, last worked in 1995, hosts a 56,000-ounce inferred gold resource and could become the mill’s next ore source, subject to further approvals and a decision to mine.

Further southwest along Victoria’s Stawell gold corridor, the company’s flagship Irvine gold project lies 130km from Wedderburn and 16km south of the Stawell gold mine, which has produced more than 5 million ounces. The longer-term growth play packs a hefty 398,000-ounce inferred resource and a separate conceptual exploration target of between 316,000 and 665,000 ounces, offering considerable scope to grow its gold inventory through further exploration.

Experienced metallurgist Marcus Binks, a former Fosterville processing manager involved in establishing Wedderburn, is expected to join the board as a non-executive director after the November 30 annual general meeting.

The timing for Aureka’s entry into production looks shrewd, coming against a backdrop of historically elevated bullion prices. The World Gold Council reported an average September-quarter gold price of US$4262 (A$6000) an ounce, providing a potentially lucrative environment for emerging producers.

By acquiring an operating mine and a scarce, underutilised processing plant, Aureka has sidestepped the lengthy and costly process of building from scratch. With a strong gold price and a pipeline of projects to feed its new mill, the company has rapidly assembled the core components of a regional Victorian gold business.

items.title: Anthropic’s trillion-dollar IPO is open to Australians. There’s a catch for small investors
paras: Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic’s trillion‑dollar IPO is open to Australians. There’s a catch for small investors Published: November 15, 2026 10:24pm EST For the second time this year, Wall Street is preparing for a blockbuster stock market debut. Shares in Anthropic – the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models – are due to start trading on the US NASDAQ stock exchange on Thursday, US time.
As with the SpaceX listing earlier this year, everyday Australian investors can be part of the action. They have until 5pm (AEDT) on Tuesday to apply for shares in Anthropic at the offer price.
Doing so doesn’t guarantee they’ll get the full amount they apply for – or any shares at all. According to Bloomberg , bankers say the offer is about six times oversubscribed.

That matters, because who gets shares at the offer price largely decides who makes money. Decades of US data show most of the gains from tech floats go to those who are allocated shares at the offer price, and that is rarely small investors. Those who buy only after the shares start trading have tended to do worse.
An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Australia is one of only a few places outside the US where retail investors can apply.
Anthropic plans to sell 825 million shares at US$70–$78 each (A$104–$115), under the ticker “ ANT ”.

Not everyone pays the same price, though. Before trading starts, shares are sold at a fixed “offer price” to investors who applied – mostly big institutional investors, plus some everyday investors through brokers. Once the shares list, anyone can buy them on the stock market, at whatever price buyers and sellers agree on.
When demand is strong, that price often jumps. The rise from the offer price to the end of the first day’s trading is known as the “pop”.
University of Florida finance professor Jay Ritter has tracked more than 9,000 American floats since 1980. Tech floats have jumped 31% on average between the offer price and the first day’s close.

In 2020, Wall Street saw a “frenzy” of tech floats, with some extraordinary pops. Shares in Airbnb, for example, more than doubled on day one. Since then, banks have been pricing the biggest deals more cautiously, though average pops remain large.

What happens after day one is much less exciting. Leave out the dot-com bubble, and tech shares bought at the offer price beat the US share market by about 26 percentage points over the next three years.
Bought at the first day’s closing price, they trailed it by about five percentage points. Almost all the gain was the pop.
When a float is popular, orders outstrip the number of shares offered and applications get scaled back.
Informed investors, often big institutions, pile into the good deals and avoid the bad ones. US evidence shows institutions are given more shares in the floats that jump most on day one.
Academic research has called the result the “ winner’s curse ”. Small investors only get a sliver of the floats that do well, but everything they asked for in the ones that flop.
In addition to the stock market listing, Anthropic has also arranged to sell US$26 billion worth of shares through private placements to Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and other tech giants.

And importantly, Anthropic is selling only a small slice of the company. Including the side deal, it is set to raise about US$87 billion, which values the whole company at about US$1.4 trillion once all shares and options are counted.
This would slightly exceed the record US$85.7 billion raised by SpaceX in its June float, even though SpaceX’s opening valuation was higher (US$1.77 trillion).
According to the US prospectus , only about 6% of Anthropic’s shares will be sold in the float. Existing investors and staff hold nearly all the rest and have agreed not to sell for up to a year.
Shareholders will have little power, as a trust and a company controlled by the founders are expected to elect the whole board.

Anthropic’s revenue rocketed from US$4.6 billion in 2025 to US$33.2 billion in the first nine months of this year. However, the company still made an operating loss of US$1.3 billion . It has also committed to about US$901 billion of future spending, mostly on computing power.

There’ll be no dividends for now, so investors only make money if the share price goes up. The shares trade only on Nasdaq and only in US dollars, so currency swings will also impact any returns for Australians.
The timing worries some. Anthropic is chasing a record float just as AI funding is starting to dry up , and there are signs investors are already losing faith in the AI story.
Read more: Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story

Many investors do little homework. One recent US study of investors’ web browsing found the typical person spends about six minutes researching a stock before trading it, looking mostly at price charts and analysts’ views rather than risk.
Six minutes isn’t much time to size up a loss-making company worth around US$1.4 trillion.

Anthropic may well turn out to be a great company. Whether it’s a good buy is a separate question. History says the gains go mostly to whoever gets in at the offer price, and small investors rarely get much.

items.title: ClearVue cracks Singapore market with major solar win

Share A A A Smart building materials company ClearVue Technologies has secured a significant commercial foothold in Asia, after receiving a letter of award for a sub-contract worth between S$500,000 and S$750,000 (A$573,000 to A$859,800) to supply a government-owned building in Singapore.
ClearVue shares jumped as much as 13 per cent to 6.9 cents on heavy turnover in mid-morning trade as investors welcomed the news.

ClearVue Technologies’ solar power-generating cladding is available in a wide range of colours, patterns and visual textures. The deal came through an established Singapore-based façade contractor and will see ClearVue’s solar cladding integrated into a large-scale public project in the city-state, potentially providing a major endorsement of the Perth-based company’s technology and its push into the lucrative Asian market.

Under the contract, ClearVue will supply an estimated 4000 square metres of its unique solar power-generating building cladding for the building’s façade. The system consists of grey-finished laminated glass panels with matching aluminium framing and is designed to deliver a combined façade peak capacity of roughly 670 kilowatts. That output will materially offset the building’s operational costs and contribute to its renewable energy targets.

Notably, the project will use a sealed-face façade, an application tailor-made for the company’s proprietary thermal bridge junction box technology. Management says the technology will keep the panels’ electronics cool and dry within the façade cavity, even in Singapore’s high-temperature equatorial climate.

ClearVue managing director and chief executive officer Doug Hunt said: “ This is a major win for ClearVue in Asia and strong commercial validation of our technology. Being selected to supply a government project in Singapore is a significant achievement, not just for this project, but for the business we have spent years building.”

The timing of the contract slots in neatly with Singapore’s aggressive push to decarbonise its built environment. The government’s Green Building Masterplan is targeting 80 per cent of its buildings by gross floor area to be “green” by 2030, with new developments intended to meet Super Low Energy standards from that same year.

Singapore’s public sector buildings have been a key part of that policy, with new government buildings required to achieve Green Mark certification since 2006. The national solar target provides another powerful tailwind, with the government aiming to deploy at least 2 gigawatts-peak of solar capacity by 2030.

Due to commercial confidentiality, ClearVue is unable to name the contractor or the specific project at this stage. However, the company notes the contractor is a serious player, forming part of a group that employs about 500 people and holds the highest possible Singapore Building and Construction Authority registration for curtain wall works, with no ceiling on tender value.

This latest contract adds to ClearVue’s growing list of international projects. It follows a A$305,000 contract for the Rio Business Centre in Cyprus and a significant subcontract to supply and install its solar products for Canva’s new global headquarters in Sydney.
The company has also recently established a regional office and showroom in Hong Kong to support its growth ambitions in the Greater Bay Area and Southern China.

The Singapore project is estimated to take 240 days to deliver. ClearVue says it has passed all necessary testing against international standards for photovoltaic module safety, reliability, performance and fire classification applicable to the project.

With its Australian-developed technology now being written into the specifications for international government infrastructure, ClearVue is steadily compiling a respectable and practical global resume. For a company looking to effectively convert entire buildings into self-contained power stations, securing a key role in one of the world’s most advanced green building markets could provide a glimpse into what future cities may look like.

items.title: Sexual misconduct inside the NSW Police Force exposed
paras: Ashlee, not her real name, spoke out about being assaulted and sexually harassed by a fellow member of the NSW Police Force just a year into her career. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma )
When Ashlee graduated from the NSW Police Academy in 2018, she was in it for the long haul.
"I was bright-eyed and bushy-tailed when I joined. I never thought that I would even have to contemplate a different career," she told 7.30.
Ashlee is still a NSW Police officer and is using a pseudonym to protect her identity.
She is currently on medical leave due to her mental health along with a physical injury and says returning to work is still "too terrifying" to contemplate.
Ashlee is one of the few police officers who reported a senior colleague for assaulting her and took her case to criminal court.
New data obtained by 7.30 under freedom of information laws shows there have been dozens of other sexual misconduct allegations made against NSW Police employees in the period between 2021 and 2025.
The workplace culture within the NSW Police Force has been under scrutiny. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton )
In that time there were 483 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees.
In the same period, there were also 67 allegations of sexual touching against NSW Police employees and 10 allegations of indecent assault.

There were also 45 allegations of rape against NSW Police employees, 17 of which were allegedly committed against their colleagues, some of these involved multiple allegations against individual officers.

According to NSW Police, a total of 36 employees were accused of rape in the past five years and of those, six police officers have been prosecuted for sexual assault. Eight of the accused officers have lost their jobs.
In its 2025 annual report the NSW Police Force said it had 15,887 officers and 4,508 administrative officers.
After graduating, Ashlee worked as a probationary constable in Sydney's northern suburbs in 2019.
In June, she attended a house party hosted by another officer in Sydney's Northern Beaches.
Among those in attendance was leading Constable Ryan Dare, who was a more experienced and higher-ranking officer from a neighbouring station.
In the past five years, there were almost 500 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees. ( ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon )
After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Ashlee alleges Dare's behaviour escalated.
"He would stand behind me, playing with my hair, hands over my shoulders, putting his head next to me and people were noticing," she said.
Other officers who were there witnessed the assault and immediately stepped in and removed Dare from the venue.
After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Constable Ryan Dare's behaviour escalated. ( ABC News: Nicole Chettle )
She was then faced with the difficult decision of whether to proceed with criminal charges against Dare.
"To think that it was another police officer that did it to me, that is not something I thought even possible when I joined the police force," she said.
Given there was CCTV of the assault and several witnesses, Ashlee decided to pursue criminal charges.
Dare was initially charged with sexual touching and faced a local court hearing, where Ashlee was cross-examined for several hours.
While the trial was ongoing, Dare was allowed to continue working as an officer at a nearby station, where Ashlee encountered him on the job.
She says he also lived in the same area and that she saw him both at work and while doing her grocery shopping.
During the legal process, Dare was allowed to continue working at a neighbouring station. ( ABC News: Floss Adams )
"If it was a normal person, they would get an AVO, but I wasn't even treated like a normal [person], wasn't even given that opportunity to do that."
Ashlee said she didn't feel like she could request an AVO to be put in place given Dare had been allowed to return to the workplace.
In a statement, NSW Police told 7.30" "The need for an AVO depends on the particular circumstances, and at the time there was no identified need for an AVO."
"AVOs are utilised where there are concerns regarding a complainant's safety or the management of ongoing risk, which had already been mitigated."
A guilty plea for the lesser charge of common assault was eventually accepted by the prosecutor and Dare was suspended with pay.
"We pushed to have it continue as a sexual touching case and ultimately that was taken away from me," Ashlee said.
Dare was sentenced to a nine-month good behaviour bond and had his conviction removed from his record after an appeal.
After his guilty plea, Dare was allowed to continue working as a police officer for another year.

NSW Police said Dare was "managed in the workplace" with restrictions in place to ensure both parties did not come into contact, which included "transferring the officer to another station and prohibiting the officer from undertaking duties in certain commands".
Ashlee said during the process that NSW Police Force leadership asked her if she would support a decision to allow Dare to keep his job, with a demotion.
It took almost four years from the day of the assault before Dare was sacked from the police force by then-Commissioner Karen Webb, as a result of the guilty plea.
Karen Webb was the first female police commissioner in NSW and ordered an independent cultural review. ( ABC News: Warwick Ford )
The following year, Ms Webb, the state's first female commissioner, launched an independent culture review of the NSW Police Force, triggered by an ABC News investigation.

The review, published in June , uncovered hundreds of reports of sexual harassment and dozens of allegations of sexual assault within the NSW Police Force, along with a longstanding culture of silence.
Ms Webb retired before the findings and recommendations were delivered but told 7.30 she always maintained the organisation had a problem with its treatment of women.
"I'd seen it over the years, and it hadn't really shifted from 38 years ago right to the end," Ms Webb told 7.30.

"It was time to do something that would actually lead to substantial change, hopefully ... for the women coming through and the women in the organisation now that have still got long careers ahead of them."
Ms Webb said she knew some senior officers were routinely preying on probationary constables.
Karen Webb retired from the top job before the final report was delivered. ( ABC News: Craig Hansen )
Ms Webb said the number of officers accused of sexual misconduct in the past five years was "appalling".

"The thing that worries me, though, is that I know from being a detective and investigating sexual assaults that we know in society only 1 in 10 or 1 in 20 women come forward to report their sexual assault," she said.
"If that's representative of the number of women that have come forward in the organisation to report their sexual assault, then that number is much higher in reality."

Former NSW Police Senior Sergeant Mel Cooper , whose story helped trigger the independent culture review in 2024, said she also believes the number of women on the force who have experienced sexual assault, sexual touching and sexual harassment is much higher than reported.
Retired senior sergeant Mel Cooper says she is not surprised by the number of sexual misconduct allegations in the force. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma )

"Every single one of them has happened to me … and the fact that every single one of them is still happening to serving police officers by serving police officers currently … that breaks my heart," Ms Cooper said.
Ms Cooper said she never reported any of the assaults or harassment during her time on the force.
"Then things happen … and you're put in a position where you have a choice to make as to whether you do come forward and report things … or whether you just put it aside."
Mel Cooper says she experienced harassment, unwanted touching and even sexual assault throughout her career. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma )
According to the culture review's final report, "very few" survey respondents felt safe reporting harmful behaviour and most commonly dealt with incidents by avoiding the perpetrator.
"We heard some stories about the targeting of probationary officers, including by field training officers who were signing off on their training and performance," the report stated.
"Participants also described unwelcome sexual touching of varying degrees of seriousness, including instances where leaders misused their rank and position of power."
Many of the culture review's 29 recommendations were aimed at fostering a safer environment for officers to report misconduct.
NSW Police said all the recommendations have been accepted by Commissioner Mal Lanyon and are being rolled out.
"The Independent Cultural Review also recognised that the NSWPF has made significant improvements in complaints handling and reporting," a statement said.
"The New South Wales Police Force takes all allegations of sexual harassment, misconduct and assault seriously … sexual assault and misconduct are never acceptable."
NSW Police says all 29 recommendations from the culture review have been accepted and are being rolled out. ( ABC News: Abubakr Sajid )
Ashlee says the experience has left her with little faith in NSW Police and the justice system to protect victims and hold perpetrators accountable.

"It has traumatised me so greatly in so many aspects of my life and even the continuation of work, that it is just absolutely not worth it for the ongoing and lifelong issues that I'm going to have for him to literally just lose his job," she said.

items.title: Small regional town fights back against proposed AI data centre
paras: Dozens of people travelled from the Ballarat region to protest the proposal of a data centre in Miners Rest. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )
Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest.
Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures.
Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres.
The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people.

Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry.
Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming.
"There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said.
"[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting."
Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )
Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires.

"Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning."
On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria.
As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline.
Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )
Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans.
He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community.
Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site.
"There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said.
Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )
Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre.
"It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said.
He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community.
"I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said.
"We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled."
Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )
In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area.
"There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said.
"A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement."
The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal.
"While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said.
"All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process."

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: November 16, 2001: The day Lleyton Hewitt became world No 1 for the first time
paras: On this day in tennis history, a young Australian, who had recently won the US Open, secured his spot at the top of the rankings for the very first time
On this day, November 16, 2001, in the ATP Masters Cup round-robin, world No 2 Lleyton Hewitt defeated fellow Australian Pat Rafter (7-5, 6-2) to secure the ATP’s No 1 ranking for the first time.

Hewitt, who had recently triumphed at the US Open , would clinch the title a few days later, defeating Sebastien Grosjean in the final (6-3, 6-3, 6-4). While his father had been a professional Australian football player and his mother a professional netball player, young Lleyton chose tennis. A year later, in 1998, the young Aussie stunned the tennis world by clinching his first ATP title before his 17th birthday, in his hometown of Adelaide.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
